Why Native Seed
Outperforms Sod
in a Drought
The deeper roots, the lower water bill, and the lawn that lasts.
Shop Native Seed

Sod sits on a shallow mat of soil. The roots are typically two to three inches deep when it leaves the farm — and in dry conditions, they don't go much deeper. That's why a sodded lawn needs constant irrigation: there's nowhere else for it to find water.
Seeded grass — particularly drought-tolerant native species — does the opposite. Buffalo grass roots can reach four to six feet deep. Blue grama and bermudagrass aren't far behind. They evolved to survive dry summers on the Great Plains and the Southwest by chasing moisture down through the soil profile, not by waiting for sprinklers.
That root depth is the entire game in a drought. A buffalo grass lawn established from seed will hold green color through a dry summer with little or no supplemental water. A sodded cool-season lawn next to it will brown out in two weeks without irrigation. Same yard, same rainfall — completely different outcomes.
